title: Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo
hook: A grammatical English sentence made of nothing but the word "buffalo".
peek: "Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo" is a correct English sentence. It works because buffalo can be a city, an animal and a verb meaning to intimidate, and it shows how much grammar our brains handle without noticing.
lede: "Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo." It looks like a typing accident, but it is a proper English sentence. The word does three jobs: Buffalo the city in New York, buffalo the animal, and buffalo the verb, meaning to bully or intimidate. Read with care, it says that bison from Buffalo, whom other Buffalo bison bully, themselves bully Buffalo bison.

bullets.text: The philosopher and computer scientist William J. Rapaport of the University at Buffalo devised the sentence in 1972. Steven Pinker later brought it to a wide audience in his 1994 book The Language Instinct.
Sentences like "The horse raced past the barn fell" lead the reader down one reading, then force a restart. The buffalo sentence is an extreme case, because word order alone has to carry the meaning.
Because buffalo works as a noun, adjective and verb, strings of almost any length can be read as grammatical. The eight-word version is simply the one that became famous.

The Chinese linguist Yuen Ren Chao wrote a short story in classical Chinese in which every syllable is pronounced "shi", with only tone telling them apart. Read aloud, it is close to impossible to follow.
Repeating "buffalo" eight times can make it stop sounding like a word at all. That loss of meaning through repetition has a name, and it happens with any word.
Making one word do many jobs is also the whole design of Toki Pona, an invented language with about 120 words, where context does much of the work.
